title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed economist Jeremy Pearce shows U.S. labor productivity growth roughly doubled to ~2.2% a year in 2019-2025 from ~1% in 2010-2019, with Compustat public-firm real revenue per worker accelerating from 0.7% to 2.2% a year. A meaningful part of the gains went to firms: sales-weighted gross margins rose from ~34% to 37% and operating margins from ~16% to 18%, consistent with a declining labor share. Firms with higher 2019 R&D intensity (not capital intensity) saw larger subsequent operating-markup growth.

insights.claim: U.S. nonfarm-business output per hour grew 1.0% a year from 2010 to 2019 and accelerated to 2.2% a year from 2019 to 2025, ending more than a decade of slow productivity growth.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: A sustained doubling of trend productivity growth supports higher potential GDP and non-inflationary growth capacity.
insights.quote: Nonfarm-business output per hour grew 1.0 percent a year from 2010 to 2019 and 2.2 percent a year from 2019 to 2025.

insights.claim: U.S. productivity growth in the late 1990s ran at about 3% a year, versus about 1% a year in 2010-2019, with the 2010s slowdown especially pronounced in manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Even the post-2019 pickup to ~2% remains below the late-1990s tech-boom pace, framing how much room an AI-era boom could have.
insights.quote: Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s.

insights.claim: Among U.S. public (Compustat) firms outside agriculture, utilities, finance, real estate and public administration, real revenue per worker growth accelerated from 0.7% a year in 2010-2019 to 2.2% a year in 2019-2025, mirroring the aggregate BLS productivity turn.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Firm-level micro data corroborate the macro productivity acceleration, reducing the odds it is a statistical artifact.
insights.quote: Real revenue per worker—sales deflated by industry output prices, divided by employment—traces the same turn, from 0.7 percent to 2.2 percent a year over the same time periods.

insights.claim: The NY Fed author concludes that the post-2019 U.S. labor productivity uptick is real because it appears consistently across both aggregate BLS data and public-firm Compustat data.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Investors skeptical of the productivity revival narrative face cross-validated evidence against them.
insights.quote: Across all datasets, the labor productivity uptick is real.

themes.theme: Who captures the gains: margins vs workers

insights.claim: Higher firm revenue per worker can be distributed either to workers via higher wages as firms compete for labor or to firms via higher profit margins, so productivity growth alone does not reveal who benefits.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Tracking margins alongside productivity is necessary to judge whether productivity gains feed earnings or labor income.
insights.quote: The additional revenue may go to workers, as firms compete for labor through higher wages, or accrue to firms in profit margins.
insights.locator: Higher revenue per worker at the firm level

insights.claim: Through the 2010s U.S. public-firm margins were flat, with gross margins growing about 0.4% a year from 2010 to 2019 and operating margins roughly flat.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: The 2010s low-productivity era coincided with stagnant margins, making the post-2019 margin expansion a regime change.
insights.quote: Through the 2010s margins were flat: gross margins grew about 0.4 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, and operating margins were roughly flat.

insights.claim: Sales-weighted gross margins of U.S. Compustat firms rose from about 34% of sales in 2019 to 37% in 2025 (1.3% growth per year), and operating margins rose from 16% to 18% (2.4% growth per year).
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Corporate margins have structurally widened since COVID, supporting elevated earnings and equity valuations if sustained.
insights.quote: on average, gross margins went from about 34 percent of sales in 2019 to 37 percent in 2025 (1.3 percent growth per year), and operating margins from 16 percent to 18 percent (2.4 percent growth per year).

insights.claim: A meaningful part of the post-2019 U.S. productivity gains has gone into wider corporate profit margins rather than to workers, consistent with an ongoing decline in the labor share of output.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: A falling labor share implies productivity gains are boosting capital income more than wages, with distributional and political implications.
insights.quote: The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output.

insights.claim: Because firms captured part of the productivity gains as margin, the productivity boom is less likely to translate into proportionally faster wage growth for workers.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Implied: margin capture may limit wage-driven inflation pressure but sharpen labor-versus-capital tension.
insights.quote: Part of the gains surfaced with wider profit margins: on a reasonable baseline, the operating margin rose over 2 percent a year from 2019 to 2025.

themes.theme: R&D and intangibles predict markup gains

insights.claim: U.S. public firms with 10% more R&D expenditure relative to sales in 2019 saw about 0.7% higher operating-markup growth over 2019-2025, and 0.5% higher over 2022-2025.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Pre-existing R&D intensity is a screen for firms that captured margin expansion in the post-COVID era.
insights.quote: firms with 10 percent more R&D expenditure relative to sales in 2019 saw about 0.7 percent higher operating-markup growth over 2019–2025, and 0.5 percent over 2022–2025.

insights.claim: Firms with higher capital intensity did not show a significant pattern of larger markup gains after 2019, suggesting returns accrued to intangible rather than physical capital intensity.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Asset-light, intangible-heavy business models have been rewarded over capital-heavy ones in margin terms.
insights.quote: Firms with higher capital intensity did not see such a significant pattern. This pattern is consistent with returns to intangible intensity rather than capital intensity.
insights.locator: Firms that entered the period with higher

insights.claim: Investment in technology and intangibles may play an important role in driving rising corporate markups, consistent with rising returns to high-tech firms since COVID.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Supports a structural tailwind for tech-heavy, R&D-intensive sectors' profitability.
insights.quote: R&D intensity appears to be an important predictor of margin growth for firms, consistent with the rising returns to high-tech firms and firms that have invested in intangibles since COVID.

insights.claim: Earlier NY Fed work found that while U.S. manufacturing productivity growth slowed in the 2010s, R&D intensity in manufacturing kept rising, an apparent R&D-productivity puzzle.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: R&D spending may pay off with a lag or show up in margins rather than in measured output.
insights.quote: In earlier work, we showed that while productivity growth in manufacturing slowed in the 2010s, R&D intensity in manufacturing continued to rise.
insights.locator: Which Firms Saw the Largest Gains?

insights.claim: It remains unresolved whether rising U.S. corporate margins are a return on significant intangible investment or purely a windfall for firms.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: If margins are windfalls rather than earned returns, they are more vulnerable to competition, regulation or mean reversion.
insights.quote: Whether these rising margins are returns to significant investment in intangibles or purely a windfall for firms is a topic to explore in future work.

insights.claim: The NY Fed study measures firm productivity as Compustat real revenue per worker (sales deflated by industry output prices, divided by employment) and excludes agriculture, utilities, finance, real estate and public administration due to known productivity-measurement challenges.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Results cover public manufacturing and services firms only, so they may not generalize to private firms or excluded sectors.
insights.quote: I drop agriculture, utilities, finance, real estate, and public administration, due to the known challenges of productivity measurement in those industries.
insights.locator: This piece studies U.S. Compustat firms

insights.claim: In the study, gross margin subtracts cost of goods sold from sales, while operating margin also subtracts SG&A, which in Compustat typically includes R&D expense.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Pearce
insights.so_what: Operating-margin gains for R&D-heavy firms occur despite R&D being expensed within overhead, strengthening the finding.
insights.quote: The gross margin subtracts the direct cost of production (cost of goods sold), while the operating margin also subtracts overhead (selling, general, and administrative expense, which in Compustat typically includes R&D).
